sources.citation: Rüfenacht, Sara & Sereina Waldis. 2020. Diachronic and areal aspects of Brokpa phonology. Himalayan Linguistics 19(1). (read for its second-hand Dakpa notes; not saved to our check folder)
sources.note: About Brokpa, not Dakpa; no use of the word stress. Reports second-hand that Hyslop & Tshering (2010: 12) describe voiceless word-final high vowels in Dakpa (akpu̥ 'crow', phuipu̥ 'male') and that Bodt (2012: 283) notes deletion of word-final high vowels in Thongrong Dakpa -- i.e. both inaccessible sources have Dakpa phonology sections.

sources.citation: Tombleson, Anette Helgestad. 2022. Grammar sketch of Tawang Monpa. Himalayan Linguistics 21(2): 105-141. doi:10.5070/H921252709 (open access, eScholarship).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online (also online with a university library login)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2 Phonology (pp. 106-110) covers consonants, vowels, and sec. 2.3 'Tone and vowel length' (p. 109-110): two-way high/low tone, contrastive only after sonorants, predictable after stops; tone not marked in the paper. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the article. (Indirect hint only: word-final vowels dropped in normal speech, e.g. /sirp/ 'yellow' = sirpo in careful speech, p. 107-108.)

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus A. 2023. East Bodish Revisited. Bulletin of Tibetology 54(1): 49-212 (whole issue PDF from Namgyal Institute of Tibetology; no text layer, scanned pp. 49-212 with tesseract).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative-historical phonology (onsets, sound laws); no statement on stress/accent (0 hits in 62k scanned words). Footnote p. 73 on Lu's (1986, 2002) Dakpa data: the Dakpa varieties Mama, Dawang (=Tawang), Wenlang, Bangxin 'basically have a distinctive high vs. low register tone onset.. all other contour tones are conditioned by phonotactics'. States (p. 69-70) that Lu 1986 and Lu 2002 remain the most complete descriptions of any Dakpa-Dzala variety.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative word lists only (Dakpa forms from Lu 2002 with tone numbers, Tawang forms from Wangchu 2002); no prose on stress.

sources.citation: van Driem, George. 2007. Dzala and Dakpa form a coherent subgroup within East Bodish, and some related thoughts. In R. Bielmeier & F. Haller (eds.), Linguistics of the Himalayas and beyond, 71-84. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. (author's PDF via the Internet Archive of himalayanlanguages.org)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. 'Phonological impressionism' (pp. 75-76): phonological analysis of Dzala and Dakpa not completed; 'There may, however, be register tone similar to the binary distinction characteristic of Dzongkha phonology'; preglottalised high-register continuant initials in both Dzala and Dakpa.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en) 'Takpa language', citing Huang Bufan (ed.) 1992 Zang-Mianyu zu yuyan cihui p. 634 for Cona Monba tones.
sources.note: Third-hand: 'Monba is a tonal language, with four contour tones: 55, 53, 35, and 31' (Cona variety); nothing on stress.

sources.note: The only modern Western phonological sketch of Dakpa proper besides Tombleson; sec. on phonology (c. pp. 5-12) gives the phoneme inventory, tone and voiceless final vowels -- the most likely place for an explicit remark on stress (Hyslop routinely comments on stress vs tone in her East Bodish work).

sources.note: Not seen. Per Bodt 2023 it describes the Mama (Lekpo, Cona county) variety of Dakpa with Chao tone letters (four surface tones); van Driem 2007 instead took Lu's 'southern dialect' to be Dzala. Jianzhi volumes have a 语音 chapter with a 声调 section; whether 重音/轻声 is discussed is unknown.
